title: GenAI Voice Mode in Programming Education
venue: Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on Computing Education Research (Koli Calling ’25)
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how novice secondary-school programmers interact with a real-time voice-enabled generative AI tutor, what kinds of spoken feedback the tutor provides, and how students perceive it as a dialogue partner. The motivation is that voice interfaces may improve accessibility for learners, including those with disabilities, but little is known about how voice-based multimodal GenAI performs in authentic programming classrooms, especially for novices.

The authors integrated a voice mode into the Tutor Kai programming environment using OpenAI’s Realtime API with GPT-4o voice capabilities. The system allowed students to speak naturally while working on Python exercises, and the tutor responded with spoken feedback informed by the student’s current code, compiler output, task description, and dialogue history. The study analyzed 1,210 audio recordings from student-AI interactions using qualitative coding, and also collected students’ perceptions through the Partner Modelling Questionnaire (PMQ).

The study took place during regular computer science lessons at a German grammar school with nine 9th-grade students who used the GenAI voice tutor over roughly four weeks while learning Python. Students primarily used the tutor for debugging and for pair-programming-like stepwise support rather than asking for full solutions. The tutor most often gave feedback about how to proceed and about mistakes, but its spoken feedback quality was uneven.

The main conclusion is that voice-based GenAI tutoring shows promise for natural, context-aware classroom support, but in its current form it is too unreliable for novice learners. Only 71.4% of feedback instances were judged correct, and the system frequently struggled to verbalize code clearly, producing confusing or incorrect spoken output. Students perceived the tutor as relatively competent and dependable, but only moderately human-like and flexible. The authors conclude that substantial improvements in spoken code explanation are needed before such tools can reliably support learners, especially those with accessibility needs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family generative AI used here via a real-time voice interface, providing multimodal conversational tutoring and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the voice-enabled tutor within Tutor Kai, powered by OpenAI’s Realtime API using GPT-4o, to support 9th-grade students learning Python through spoken dialogue and feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In an authentic classroom case study, the GenAI voice tutor’s feedback quality was limited: 71.4% of 416 feedback instances were judged correct, while 28.6% were incorrect. The tutor most often provided knowledge on how to proceed (70.4%, 293/416) and knowledge about mistakes (36.3%, 151/416), but struggled particularly when verbalizing programming code elements.
findings.measure: Correctness and type of spoken programming feedback outputs

findings.finding_summary: Students primarily used the voice tutor for debugging and pair-programming-like support rather than asking for full solutions. Among 309 interaction prompts, debugging appeared in 56.3% (174/309) and pair programming in 20.1% (62/309), while explicit solution requests were absent (0.0%).
findings.measure: Student use patterns in programming support interactions

findings.finding_summary: Students’ perceptions of the voice tutor as a dialogue partner were moderate overall on the PMQ, with high ratings for competence/dependability but lower, neutral-area ratings for human-likeness and communicative flexibility. Specifically, the overall PMQ mean was 4.23 (SD=1.24), competence and dependability was 5.65 (SD=0.21), human-likeness was 3.41 (SD=0.52), and communicative flexibility was 3.63 (SD=0.61) on a 7-point scale.
findings.measure: Partner Modelling Questionnaire (PMQ) perceptions of competence, human-likeness, and communicative flexibility
findings.effect_size: M=4.23, SD=1.24 overall; M=5.65, SD=0.21 competence/dependability; M=3.41, SD=0.52 human-likeness; M=3.63, SD=0.61 communicative flexibility

quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative case study in an authentic classroom with a very small sample (n=9), not an RCT or QED. It provides useful empirical evidence on interaction patterns and perceived feedback quality, but causal claims about learning effectiveness are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mixed results: students engaged productively with the tool, but nearly a third of feedback instances were incorrect and no direct learning gains or standardized outcome effects were reported. Overall impact on student outcomes is therefore unclear.
